contentBlocks.text: Yesterday you learned why atoms bond. Today: ionic bonding, the transfer of electrons!

Ionic bonding happens when one atom transfers an electron (or electrons) to another atom, creating two oppositely-charged ions (connecting to last week's ion content) that attract each other through electrostatic force. When sodium gives its 1 valence electron to chlorine, sodium becomes a positive Na⁺ ion (having lost a negative charge) and chlorine becomes a negative Cl⁻ ion (having gained one), and the resulting attraction between opposite charges forms the ionic bond in table salt, NaCl. Explain why the sodium ion ends up with a positive charge and the chlorine ion ends up with a negative charge after this electron transfer.
You just learned how ionic bonding actually works! Tomorrow we'll learn about covalent bonding, a different way atoms connect.

objectives: Describe ionic bonding as electron transfer creating oppositely-charged ions
Explain why sodium becomes positively charged and chlorine becomes negatively charged
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review yesterday's octet-rule work briefly.
2. Introduce ionic bonding using the NaCl example.
3. Have the child explain the resulting charges.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's covalent-bonding lesson.
differentiationTips: Struggling: remind the child that a neutral atom has equal protons and electrons, so losing a negative electron leaves more protons than electrons (net positive), and gaining one does the opposite
Ready for more: ask the child to predict the ionic compound formed between magnesium (2 valence electrons) and chlorine, including how many chlorine atoms would be needed
This connects directly back to last week's ion content, showing WHY an atom becomes an ion in the first place through real chemical bonding
teacherGuide.answerKey: A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons (positive) and electrons (negative). Sodium loses its 1 valence electron, leaving one more proton than electrons, giving it a net positive charge (Na⁺). Chlorine gains that electron, leaving one more electron than protons, giving it a net negative charge (Cl⁻).
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses NGSS Grade 9-10 standard HS-PS1-3: analyzing bonding based on electrostatic forces between electrons and nuclei, continuing this week's chemical-bonding thread.
